notes.heading: Emission spectra and the EM spectrum
points: Excited atoms emit photons when electrons fall from higher to lower energy levels; the photon carries the energy difference between the two levels.
A continuous spectrum has all wavelengths merged. A line spectrum has only certain separate lines, characteristic of each element.
Energy and frequency increase as wavelength decreases: gamma rays are short wavelength, high frequency, high energy; radio and microwaves are the opposite.
Flame tests work by atomic emission: the flame promotes electrons, and falling back gives visible photons of certain wavelengths.

notes.heading: Hydrogen line spectrum and energy levels
points: Each line has one wavelength, so one exact energy. This shows electron energies are discrete (quantized), not continuous.
Lines get closer together at higher energy: the energy levels converge as n increases.
Falling to n = 1 gives UV, to n = 2 gives visible light, to n = 3 gives infrared.
A bigger drop releases a higher-energy photon: n = 6 to 2 gives violet (short wavelength), n = 3 to 2 gives red.
Electrons absorb or release only the exact energy gap between levels; too little energy and they do not move.

notes.heading: Main energy levels and electron capacity
points: The main energy level is numbered by the integer n = 1, 2, 3 and so on; higher n means higher energy, further from the nucleus.
Maximum electrons in level n = 2n².
So n = 1 holds 2, n = 2 holds 8, n = 3 holds 18, n = 4 holds 32.
The ground state is n = 1, the lowest energy; higher levels are excited states.

notes.heading: Sublevels s, p, d, f
points: Each main level splits into sublevels of increasing energy: s < p < d < f.
Level n has n types of sublevel: n = 1 has s only, n = 2 has s and p, n = 3 adds d, n = 4 adds f.
Orbitals per sublevel: s = 1, p = 3, d = 5, f = 7. Each level has n² orbitals in total.
The s orbital is spherical; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with three p orbitals along x, y and z.

notes.heading: Orbitals and filling electron configurations
points: An orbital is a region where an electron is likely to be found and holds at most two electrons of opposite spin (Pauli).
Aufbau: lowest-energy orbitals fill first. Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. Ions up to Z = 36 are assessed.
Hund: degenerate orbitals each get one electron, all with the same spin, before any pairs up.
Condensed form = previous noble gas in brackets plus valence electrons, e.g. Mn is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵.
Cr is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and Cu is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰: half-full or full d sublevel is more stable.
Atoms lose 4s electrons before 3d when forming ions, e.g. Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.

notes.heading: Convergence limit and ionization
points: At high frequency the spectral lines converge; the convergence limit is the point where the electron is removed, i.e. ionization.
First IE of one atom: find f from c = fλ, then E = hf (or E = hc/λ). c ≈ 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s.
Convert to kJ mol⁻¹: multiply the energy per atom by 6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹, then divide by 1000.
Worked result: hydrogen converges at 9.12×10⁻⁸ m, giving 2.18×10⁻¹⁸ J, or about 1.31×10³ kJ mol⁻¹.
Reverse: from IE per mole, divide by Avogadro's constant and 1000 conversion to joules, then use λ = hc/E.

notes.heading: Ionization energy trends and successive IEs
points: First IE generally decreases down a group (more shielding) and increases across a period (more nuclear charge, similar shielding).
Dip from group 2 to 3 (Be to B, Mg to Al): the single p electron is higher in energy and shielded by the s² pair.
Dip from group 15 to 16 (N to O): paired electrons in oxygen's p orbital repel, so one is easier to remove.
Successive IEs always rise, because fewer electrons remain for the same protons and repulsion falls.
A big jump shows removal from a new inner main level; the number of electrons before the jump equals the group's valence electrons.
Worked example: 403 then 2633 kJ mol⁻¹ shows one valence electron, so group 1.

definitions.definition: Pattern of wavelengths of light given out when excited atoms release photons as electrons fall to lower energy levels.
definitions.trap: Do not confuse with absorption spectrum, where dark lines appear against a continuous background.

definitions.definition: A spectrum containing all wavelengths of light in a range, with no gaps or separate lines.
definitions.trap: Gas discharge tubes give line spectra, not continuous ones.

definitions.definition: A spectrum of separate lines, each at one specific wavelength, characteristic of an element and showing discrete energy levels.
definitions.trap: Saying lines are colours of the whole atom rather than individual electron transitions.

definitions.definition: A quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy, with energy proportional to its frequency, E = hf.
definitions.trap: Energy is proportional to frequency but inversely proportional to wavelength.

definitions.definition: The lowest energy state of an atom, in which electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (n = 1 for hydrogen).
definitions.trap: Excited states are n = 2 and above; they are not the ground state.

definitions.definition: A region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron; holds at most two electrons.
definitions.trap: An orbital is not a fixed orbit or path of the electron.

definitions.definition: Orbitals within the same sublevel that have the same energy.
definitions.trap: 2p and 3p orbitals are not degenerate; they differ in energy.

definitions.definition: An atomic orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.
definitions.trap: Do not mix up with Hund's rule, which concerns singly filling degenerate orbitals.

definitions.definition: Degenerate orbitals in a sublevel are each singly occupied before any is doubly occupied, and single electrons have the same spin.
definitions.trap: Pairing electrons in one p orbital while others are empty breaks this rule.

definitions.definition: Electrons fill the lowest available energy orbitals first, before higher-energy orbitals are occupied.
definitions.trap: 4s fills before 3d, but Cr and Cu are exceptions.

definitions.definition: The minimum energy required to remove one electron from a neutral gaseous atom in its ground state: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.
definitions.trap: Omitting state symbols or 'gaseous'; first IE is per atom (or per mole in kJ mol⁻¹).
